column9: stem
column28: explanation
column29: hint

column9: How do plants get the food they need to live and grow?
column14: They eat other organisms, so they are heterotrophs
column15: They make their own food, so they are autotrophs
column16: They absorb food from dead material, so they are decomposers
column17: They take food from a living host, so they are parasites
column28: Plants are autotrophs: they make their own sugar using light energy. A common mistake is thinking plants get their food from the soil; roots take in water and minerals, not food.
column29: Auto- means self. Who makes a plant's food?

column9: Plant cell walls are made mostly of which substance?
column28: Plant cell walls are made of cellulose. Chitin is the cell wall material of fungi, and peptidoglycan is found in bacteria walls, so those are the common mix-ups.
column29: It is the same tough fiber found in cotton, paper and the strings of celery.

column9: Plants use the energy in sunlight to make their own sugar. This process is called ___.
column28: Photosynthesis uses light energy to make sugar. Cellular respiration is the common wrong answer; respiration breaks sugar down to release energy instead of making it.
column29: Photo- means light, and synthesis means putting something together.

column9: Which organelle in a leaf cell captures light energy to make food?
column28: Chloroplasts capture light and make sugar. Mitochondria are the common mix-up; they release energy from sugar, and plant cells have both.
column29: Its name starts with the same word part as the green pigment in leaves.

column9: Which green pigment absorbs the light that plants use to make food?
column28: Chlorophyll is the green pigment that absorbs light for photosynthesis. Melanin colors skin and hemoglobin carries oxygen in blood; chitin is not a pigment at all.
column29: Chloro- means green.

column9: Which pair of words describes EVERY plant, from a tiny moss to a giant redwood?
column28: All plants are made of many cells, and those cells have a nucleus, so plants are multicellular eukaryotes. Picking unicellular is the common mistake; single-celled green organisms are protists, not plants.
column29: Can you see a moss without a microscope? Do plant cells have a nucleus?

column9: About how many species of plants have scientists described?
column28: Scientists have described nearly 400,000 plant species, and most of them are flowering plants. Students often guess far too low because they only think of the plants they see every day.
column29: It is a very large number, but less than half a million.

column9: What is the main job of vascular tissue in a plant?
column17: Moving water and food through the plant
column28: Vascular tissue is the plant's plumbing: it moves water and food from one part of the plant to another. Absorbing sunlight is the job of chlorophyll in the leaves, which is the common mix-up.
column29: Think of the pipes in a building.

column9: The vascular tissue that carries sugar made in the leaves to the rest of the plant is called ___.
column28: Phloem carries sugar (food) from the leaves to the stems, roots and fruits. Xylem is the common mix-up; xylem carries water up from the roots.
column29: Its name sounds like it starts with an f, but it is spelled with ph.

column9: A celery stalk is placed in a cup of blue-dyed water. A few hours later, blue lines run up the stalk and into the leaves. Which tissue carried the dyed water?
column28: Xylem carries water up from the bottom of the plant, so the dye followed the xylem. Phloem is the common wrong answer; phloem moves sugar, mostly away from the leaves.
column29: Which tissue moves water upward?

column9: Mosses are called nonvascular plants because they...
column17: have no cells with a nucleus
column28: Nonvascular means no vascular tissue, so mosses have no xylem or phloem. Mosses are still green, have cellulose walls and are eukaryotes, so the other choices describe things mosses do have.
column29: Look at the word: non- means not. Not what?

column9: The nonvascular plants, called bryophytes, include mosses, liverworts and ___.
column28: The three groups of nonvascular plants are mosses, liverworts and hornworts. Writing ferns is the common mistake; ferns have vascular tissue.
column29: This plant grows tiny horn-shaped stalks.

column9: Horsetails and whisk ferns belong to which plant group?
column28: Horsetails and whisk ferns, like ferns, have vascular tissue but reproduce with spores, so they are seedless vascular plants. Calling them nonvascular is the common mistake because they have no seeds or flowers.
column29: They are grouped with the ferns.

column9: What does the word gymnosperm mean?
column28: Gymno- means naked and -sperm means seed, so a gymnosperm's seeds are not wrapped inside a fruit. "Seed in a container" is the meaning of angiosperm, which is the common mix-up.
column29: Gymno- comes from the same Greek word as gymnasium, where ancient Greek athletes trained without clothes.

column9: Angiosperms are also known as...
column28: Angiosperms are the flowering plants. Cone-bearing plants are gymnosperms, which is the most common mix-up.
column29: Think of roses, sunflowers and apple trees.

column9: In an angiosperm, which structure produces the fruit that surrounds the seeds?
column28: In angiosperms, flowers produce fruit, and the seeds develop inside it. Students sometimes think fruit just grows from a branch, but every apple or acorn started as part of a flower.
column29: Before an apple tree has apples in the fall, what does it have in the spring?

column9: Where do the seeds of a blue spruce tree form?
column15: In brown dots under its needles
column17: On the scales of its cones
column28: Spruces are gymnosperms, so their seeds form on the scales of cones. Saying "inside a fruit" is the common mistake; only angiosperms make fruit.
column29: What woody structures do you find under a spruce tree?

column9: A fern makes no seeds. The brown dots on the underside of its fronds release tiny ___ that can grow into new plants.
column28: The brown dots on a fern frond hold spores. Writing seeds is the common mistake; ferns are seedless plants.
column29: Mosses use these too.

column9: Which plant part anchors the plant and absorbs water and minerals from the soil?
column28: Roots anchor the plant and absorb water and minerals, and many roots also store food. The stem is the common wrong choice; it carries water up but does not take it in from the soil.
column29: Which part is underground?

column9: In a typical plant, where does most photosynthesis happen?
column28: Leaves are flat and full of chloroplasts, so most photosynthesis happens there. Roots are the common wrong answer; they are underground in the dark and cannot photosynthesize.
column29: Which part is broad and green and faces the sun?

column9: What does the stem do for a plant?
column14: It takes in water and minerals from the soil
column15: It makes the seeds and fruit
column16: It holds the plant up and carries water and food between the roots and leaves
column17: It releases spores into the air
column28: The stem supports the plant and contains the xylem and phloem that connect roots to leaves. Taking water from the soil is the root's job, which is the common mix-up.
column29: The stem sits between the roots and the leaves.

column9: Tiny pores in the surface of a leaf that let gases move in and out are called ___.
column28: Stomata are the small openings in a leaf. Students sometimes write chloroplasts, but chloroplasts are inside cells and make food; they are not openings.
column29: The word comes from the Greek word for mouth.

column9: Each tiny pore in a leaf is surrounded by two curved cells that swell or shrink to open and close it. These are called ___ cells.
column28: Guard cells open and close each pore, guarding how much gas and water vapor moves through. Writing epidermal is too general; guard cells are the special pair around each pore.
column29: Their job is to protect the opening, like a security guard at a door.

column9: What is the job of the waxy cuticle that covers a leaf?
column14: It keeps water from evaporating out of the leaf
column15: It soaks up water from the air
column16: It makes food for the plant
column17: It carries sugar to the roots
column28: The cuticle is a waxy waterproof layer that slows water loss. Students often think it soaks up water, but wax does the opposite: it seals water in.
column29: Think of how a waxed car makes water bead up and run off.

column9: How many cotyledons (seed leaves) does a monocot seed have?
column28: Mono- means one, so a monocot has 1 cotyledon. Dicots have 2, which is the common mix-up.
column29: Look at the prefix mono-.

column9: A leaf has veins that run side by side in straight lines from its base to its tip. Which kind of plant most likely grew this leaf?
column28: Parallel veins are a monocot trait, like a blade of grass or a corn leaf. Dicots have branching, net-like veins, which is the common mix-up.
column29: Think of a blade of grass.

column9: Which of these plants is a monocot?
column28: Lilies are monocots: flower parts in 3s and parallel leaf veins. Sunflowers, oaks and beans are dicots with net-veined leaves.
column29: Count the petals of this flower: they come in threes.

column9: Which plant group has the most species?
column28: Angiosperms are by far the largest group of plants. Students sometimes pick conifers because Wisconsin forests have so many pines, but there are far more kinds of flowering plants.
column29: Think of how many kinds of grasses, flowers, fruits and vegetables there are.

column9: Which tree is a gymnosperm?
column28: Eastern hemlock is a conifer with needles and small cones, so it is a gymnosperm. Oaks, maples and apples all have flowers and fruit, so they are angiosperms.
column29: Which tree has needles and cones?

column9: All plants reproduce with seeds.
column28: False. Mosses and ferns reproduce with spores and make no seeds. Only gymnosperms and angiosperms make seeds, so assuming every plant has seeds is the common mistake.
column29: Think about mosses and ferns.

column9: Which statement about the body of a moss is true?
column15: It has flowers hidden under its leaves
column17: It has no true roots, stems or leaves
column28: Mosses have no true roots, stems or leaves because those organs need vascular tissue. Moss has tiny leaf-like parts, so students often think it has real leaves.
column29: True roots, stems and leaves contain vascular tissue.

column9: What is inside a seed?
column14: A single cell with no stored food
column15: Only water for the new plant
column16: A tiny young plant (embryo) and stored food, wrapped in a protective coat
column17: Pollen that will grow into a flower
column28: A seed holds an embryo plus stored food inside a seed coat. A single cell with no stored food describes a spore, which is the common mix-up.
column29: When you split a bean seed open, you can see a tiny plant.

column9: In seed plants, pollen grains carry what to the part of the plant that holds the eggs?
column28: Pollen carries sperm cells to the eggs. Students sometimes think pollen is food for the seed, but its job is to deliver the sperm.
column29: Pollen is the male part of plant reproduction.

column9: Which plant group has vascular tissue and seeds but no flowers?
column28: Gymnosperms have vascular tissue and seeds, but their seeds form in cones instead of flowers. Angiosperms are the common wrong answer; they are the ones with flowers.
column29: Seeds yes, flowers no. Think of a pine.

column9: The flower parts of a dicot usually come in multiples of what number?
column28: Dicot flowers usually have parts in 4s or 5s. Flower parts in 3s is the monocot pattern, which is the common mix-up.
column29: Monocots use 3. Dicots use a different pattern.

column9: A carrot is one thick main root that grows straight down and stores food. What type of root is it?
column28: One large main root that grows deep is a taproot. Fibrous roots are many thin roots of about the same size, which is the common mix-up.
column29: This root has one main tap that goes deep.

column9: When you pull up a clump of lawn grass, you see a mass of many thin, branching roots spread out near the surface. What type of roots are these?
column28: Many thin, branching, shallow roots are fibrous roots. Taproot is the common mistake; a taproot is one thick main root.
column29: No root is bigger than the others; they look like a mop of fibers.

column9: Which of these organisms belongs in Kingdom Plantae?
column14: A clump of moss on a rock
column28: Moss is a multicellular eukaryote that photosynthesizes, so it is a plant. A mushroom is a fungus, which is the common mix-up because mushrooms grow out of the ground like plants.
column29: Which one is green and makes its own food?

column9: Plants store most of the extra sugar they make as which substance?
column28: Plants store extra sugar as starch, as in potatoes and corn. Glycogen is how animals and fungi store sugar, which is the common mix-up.
column29: Potatoes and rice are full of this carbohydrate.

column9: Match each plant group to an example from Wisconsin.
column28: Sphagnum moss has no vascular tissue, ostrich fern has vascular tissue but spores, balsam fir makes seeds in cones and wild geranium has flowers. Swapping the fern and the moss is the common mistake.
column29: Start with the one that flowers, then the one with cones.

column9: Match each part of a leaf to its description.
column14: Petiole :: The stalk that connects the leaf to the twig
column15: Lobe :: A section of the leaf separated from the rest by a deep indent
column16: Margin :: The outer edge of the leaf
column17: Blade :: The broad, flat part of the leaf
column28: The petiole is the stalk, a lobe is a section between indents, the margin is the edge and the blade is the flat part. Mixing up margin and lobe is the common slip.
column29: Margin means edge, as in the margin of a page.

column9: Match each leaf arrangement to how the leaves attach at a node (the spot where leaves grow from a twig).
column14: Alternate :: One leaf at each node
column15: Opposite :: Two leaves at each node, across from each other
column16: Whorled :: Three or more leaves at each node
column28: Alternate is one leaf per node, opposite is two across from each other and whorled is three or more. Calling a single leaf per node opposite is the common mistake.
column29: Opposite leaves face each other.

column9: Which gas do plants take in from the air to make sugar?
column28: Plants take in carbon dioxide and use it to build sugar during photosynthesis, then release oxygen. Saying oxygen is the common mistake; oxygen is what plants give off.
column29: You breathe this gas out, and plants take it in.

column9: Most Wisconsin gymnosperms, such as pines and spruces, keep their green needles all winter. Plants like this are called...
column28: Plants that stay green all year are evergreen. Deciduous plants, such as maples and oaks, drop their leaves in fall, which is the common mix-up.
column29: They are green every season.

column9: Seaweeds such as kelp are members of Kingdom Plantae.
column28: False. Kelp and other algae photosynthesize, but they are plant-like protists, not plants. They have no roots, stems, leaves or vascular tissue. Assuming anything green that photosynthesizes is a plant is the common mistake.
column29: Which kingdom holds the algae?

column9: A student finds a tiny green plant, about 2 cm tall, on a damp log. It has no flowers, no cones, and when a thin slice is viewed under a microscope, there is no xylem or phloem. Which group does it belong to?
column28: No xylem or phloem means nonvascular, like a moss or liverwort. Seedless vascular is the common wrong answer; ferns have no seeds either, but they do have vascular tissue.
column29: The microscope slice is the deciding clue.

column9: A moss has no xylem. How does water get to the cells at the top of a moss plant?
column14: It travels up through phloem tubes
column15: It is pumped up by the roots
column16: It is made by the chloroplasts
column17: It slowly soaks from cell to cell
column28: Without vascular tissue, water moves slowly from cell to cell, which is why mosses stay short. Phloem is the common wrong answer, but mosses have no phloem either.
column29: Mosses have no pipes at all.

column9: The coast redwood is the tallest plant on Earth, growing over 100 meters high. Which feature makes such great height possible?
column14: Spores that drift up to the top branches
column15: A lack of any waxy coating on its needles
column16: Vascular tissue that carries water from the roots all the way to the top
column17: Leaves that absorb water from the air
column28: Xylem carries water from the roots to the highest needles, so vascular plants can grow tall. Plants without vascular tissue, such as mosses, stay very short. Thinking that leaves soak up their water from the air is a common mistake.
column29: Water has to travel a long way up.

column9: Which trait do ferns have that mosses do NOT?
column15: Vascular tissue with true roots, stems and leaves
column28: Ferns have vascular tissue and true roots, stems and leaves; mosses do not. Spores is the common wrong choice because both ferns and mosses use spores.
column29: Both are seedless. What makes a fern taller?

column9: Which trait separates gymnosperms from ferns?
column28: Gymnosperms make seeds and ferns do not. Vascular tissue is the common wrong answer; both groups have it.
column29: Find the trait that only one of the two groups has.

column9: Which pair of structures is found ONLY in angiosperms?
column28: Only angiosperms make flowers and fruit. Xylem and phloem is the common mistake; every vascular plant has those, including ferns and pines.
column29: Angiosperm means seed in a container.

column9: Put these plant groups in order from the first to evolve to the most recent. Each group added a new feature.
column14: Angiosperms (vascular tissue, seeds in fruit, flowers)
column28: Nonvascular plants came first, then vascular tissue appeared (ferns), then seeds (gymnosperms), then flowers and fruit (angiosperms). Putting gymnosperms after angiosperms is the common slip.
column29: Each step adds one feature to the one before it.

column9: Which of these plants reproduce with spores instead of seeds? Select all that apply.
column28: Mosses, ferns and liverworts are seedless, so they use spores. Pine, tulip and corn are seed plants. Leaving out the liverwort is the common mistake.
column29: Find the plants that have no cones and no flowers.

column9: Which of these are angiosperms? Select all that apply.
column28: Maple, corn, oak and trillium all have flowers and fruit (corn kernels and acorns are fruits). White pine is a gymnosperm and moss is nonvascular. Leaving out corn is the common mistake because its flowers are small and hard to notice.
column29: Corn and oak trees do flower, even if the flowers are small.

column9: Which of these features help plants survive on dry land? Select all that apply.
column14: A waxy cuticle on the leaves
column19: Sperm that must swim through water
column28: The cuticle holds water in, vascular tissue moves water, seeds protect the embryo and pollen carries sperm without water. Picking swimming sperm is the common mistake; needing water to reproduce is a limit on land, not a help.
column29: Which features solve a problem that dry air creates?

column9: Which observations would show that a plant is a dicot? Select all that apply.
column15: Its leaves have net-like, branching veins
column17: Its stem has vascular bundles scattered all through it
column28: Two cotyledons, net veins and a taproot are dicot traits. Petals in 3s and scattered bundles are monocot traits, so choosing those is the common mistake.
column29: Di- means two. Monocots have parallel veins and parts in 3s.

column9: A student cuts across a corn stem and sees the vascular bundles scattered all through it, not in a ring. What does this show?
column28: Scattered vascular bundles are a monocot trait. Dicots have their bundles in a ring. Saying nonvascular is a mistake; the bundles ARE vascular tissue.
column29: Which group has bundles in a ring, and which has them scattered?

column9: Wild geranium, a Wisconsin wildflower, has flowers with 5 petals. Based on this clue, what kind of plant is it most likely to be?
column28: Flower parts in 4s or 5s point to a dicot. Monocot is the common wrong answer; monocot flower parts come in 3s.
column29: Is 5 a multiple of 3?

column9: A student cuts open an apple and finds the seeds inside. A pine cone has its seeds sitting on top of its scales. Which statement explains the difference?
column14: The apple tree is an angiosperm with seeds inside a fruit; the pine is a gymnosperm with naked seeds
column15: Both are gymnosperms, but the apple seeds are younger
column16: The apple tree is a gymnosperm and the pine is an angiosperm
column17: The pine cone is a fruit, just a dry one
column28: Angiosperm seeds are enclosed in a fruit, and gymnosperm seeds are naked on cone scales. Calling a pine cone a fruit is the common mistake; cones do not come from flowers.
column29: Which group has seeds in a container?

column9: Mosses need a film of water to reproduce, but pines and apple trees do not. What lets seed plants reproduce without water?
column14: Their seeds can swim to the eggs
column15: They have no sperm or eggs
column16: Their roots carry the sperm up from the soil
column17: Pollen carries their sperm through the air or on animals
column28: In seed plants, pollen carries the sperm, so the sperm does not have to swim. Thinking seed plants do not use sperm and eggs at all is a common mistake.
column29: How does the sperm of a pine tree travel?

column9: Why do mosses need water to reproduce?
column14: Their seeds must soak before they sprout
column15: Their sperm must swim through water to reach the eggs
column17: Their flowers only open when wet
column28: Moss sperm swims through a thin film of water, such as rain or dew, to reach an egg. Mosses have no seeds or flowers, so those choices describe parts mosses do not have.
column29: Mosses have no pollen.

column9: Which statement best compares a spore and a seed?
column14: A seed holds an embryo and stored food in a coat; a spore is a single cell with no stored food
column15: A spore holds an embryo and stored food; a seed is a single cell
column16: Spores and seeds are the same thing with different names
column17: Spores are made by flowers and seeds are made by ferns
column28: A seed is a whole package: a tiny plant, food and a coat. A spore is just one cell. Swapping the two is the common mistake.
column29: Which one can you split open to see a tiny plant?

column9: A student ties a clear plastic bag over the leaves of a potted plant. The next day, water droplets cover the inside of the bag. Where did most of this water leave the plant?
column15: Through the stomata in the leaves
column28: Water vapor escapes mostly through the open stomata. The cuticle is the common wrong answer; it is waxy and holds water in.
column29: Water vapor needs an opening to get out of the leaf.

column9: A cactus lives in the desert. Which feature of its outer surface would help it most?
column14: Many stomata that stay open all day
column15: A thin outer surface with no coating
column28: A thick cuticle seals water in, which matters most where water is scarce. Many open stomata is the common wrong choice; that would let water escape all day.
column29: What would keep water from escaping in dry heat?

column9: On a typical leaf, such as a maple leaf, where are most of the stomata found?
column16: On the underside of the leaf
column28: Most stomata are on the shaded underside, where less water evaporates. Students often guess the top because that side faces the sun, but stomata there would lose more water.
column29: Which side of a leaf is shaded and cooler?

column9: Put the steps in order to show how water travels through a plant.
column14: Water vapor leaves through the stomata
column15: Water rises through the xylem in the stem
column16: Water reaches the cells of the leaf
column17: Water moves into the xylem in the root
column18: Water from the soil enters the root hairs
column28: Water enters the roots, moves up the xylem through the stem to the leaves, and escapes as vapor through the stomata. Putting the stomata step first is the common slip; that is where water leaves, not where it enters.
column29: Start underground and finish in the air.

column9: Put the steps in order to show how a flowering plant makes a new plant.
column15: The seed is carried away from the parent plant
column16: Sperm from the pollen fertilizes an egg
column17: The seed sprouts into a new plant
column18: Part of the flower grows into a fruit with seeds inside
column28: Pollination comes first, then fertilization, then the fruit and seed develop, then the seed is spread and finally it sprouts. Putting fruit before fertilization is the common slip.
column29: Nothing can grow into a seed until an egg has been fertilized.

column9: Corn plants grow "prop roots" out of the stem above the ground to brace the tall plant. Roots that grow from a stem like this are called...
column28: Roots that grow from a stem, leaf or another unusual spot are adventitious roots. Fibrous is the common wrong answer; corn does have fibrous roots in the soil, but the prop roots grow from the stem.
column29: This root type is named for roots that grow from an unexpected place.

column9: Plants make their own food, but they also need minerals such as nitrogen and potassium. How does a tomato plant get these minerals?
column14: Its leaves make them during photosynthesis
column15: Its stomata take them in from the air
column16: It eats insects that land on it
column17: Its roots absorb them from the soil
column28: Roots absorb minerals dissolved in soil water. Photosynthesis is the common wrong answer; it makes sugar, not minerals. This is why gardeners add fertilizer to the soil.
column29: Why do gardeners add fertilizer to the soil?

column9: A biologist finds a new organism. It is multicellular, has chloroplasts and cellulose cell walls, has xylem and phloem, and makes seeds inside fruits. How should it be classified?
column28: The traits fit a plant, and seeds inside fruits mean angiosperm. Gymnosperm is the common wrong choice; gymnosperms make seeds but never fruit.
column29: Seeds inside fruit is the last clue.

column9: Which set of traits would tell you an organism is NOT a plant?
column14: It is multicellular and has a nucleus in each cell
column15: It has chloroplasts and makes sugar
column16: It absorbs food from dead material and has cell walls made of chitin
column17: It has cell walls made of cellulose
column28: Absorbing food and chitin cell walls describe a fungus. The other choices all describe plants. Picking "multicellular" is a common mistake, but plants are multicellular too.
column29: Which choice describes a mushroom?

column9: In a cross section of a dicot root, the xylem forms the shape of the letter ___.
column28: In dicot roots, the xylem forms an X shape in the center. In monocot roots the vascular bundles form a ring, which is the common mix-up.
column29: Picture four arms of xylem meeting in the center of the root.

column9: Ferns have true roots, stems and leaves.
column28: True. Ferns have vascular tissue, so they have true roots, stems and leaves. Students often think ferns are like mosses because both use spores, but mosses lack true organs.
column29: True roots, stems and leaves go with vascular tissue.

column9: Under a microscope, a student counts 36 stomata in a field of view that covers 0.2 mm² of a leaf's underside. How many stomata are there per mm²?
column28: Stomata per mm² = 36 ÷ 0.2 = 180. A common mistake is multiplying 36 × 0.2 = 7.2, which gives fewer stomata than were counted.
column29: 0.2 mm² is only part of 1 mm². Will 1 mm² hold more or fewer stomata?

column9: A carrot stores sugar in its root. Put the steps in order to show how sugar gets there.
column14: Sugar travels down through the phloem in the stem
column15: Sugar is made in the chloroplasts of the leaves
column16: Sugar moves into the phloem in the leaf
column17: Sugar is stored in the root as starch
column28: Sugar is made in the leaves, loaded into the phloem, carried down the stem and stored in the root. Starting in the root is the common slip; roots store sugar but cannot make it.
column29: Start where the sugar is made.

column9: On a hot, dry afternoon, the guard cells of a corn plant close its stomata. What is the most likely effect?
column14: The plant loses more water and makes more sugar
column15: More carbon dioxide gets in, so photosynthesis speeds up
column16: The plant loses less water, but less carbon dioxide gets in, so photosynthesis slows
column17: The plant stops needing water for the rest of the day
column28: Closed stomata save water, but carbon dioxide also comes in through the stomata, so photosynthesis slows. Missing this trade-off is the common mistake: closing the pores helps one thing and hurts another.
column29: Stomata let gases in and out. Which gas does photosynthesis need?

column9: A student finds a horsetail with no seeds or flowers and says, "It reproduces with spores, so it must be a moss." What is wrong with this reasoning?
column14: Horsetails have vascular tissue, so they are seedless vascular plants; using spores does not make a plant a moss
column15: Nothing is wrong; every plant that uses spores is a moss
column16: Horsetails make seeds, so they are gymnosperms
column17: Horsetails have flowers, so they are angiosperms
column28: Ferns, horsetails and mosses all use spores, so spores alone cannot tell you which group. Vascular tissue is the deciding trait. Using one shared trait to classify is the common mistake.
column29: Mosses and ferns both use spores. What trait separates them?

column9: The tamarack is a Wisconsin tree with needles that turn gold and fall off every autumn. It makes its seeds in small cones and never has flowers. Which group is it in?
column14: Angiosperm, because it drops its leaves in the fall
column15: Seedless vascular plant, because it loses its needles
column16: Nonvascular plant, because it has needles instead of leaves
column17: Gymnosperm, because it makes seeds in cones and has no flowers or fruit
column28: Classification depends on seeds in cones versus fruit, not on whether leaves fall off. Tamarack is a deciduous gymnosperm. Thinking every gymnosperm must be evergreen is the common mistake.
column29: Losing leaves is not the trait that decides the group. What about its seeds?

column9: A sweetbay magnolia has large white flowers. Later, a lumpy, cone-shaped structure forms that holds its seeds. A student says, "It has a cone, so it is a gymnosperm." Which response is correct?
column14: It is a gymnosperm, because anything shaped like a cone is a cone
column15: It is an angiosperm: it has flowers, and the cone-shaped structure is a fruit that grew from the flower
column16: It is both a gymnosperm and an angiosperm
column17: It is a seedless vascular plant, because its seeds are hidden
column28: Flowers are found only in angiosperms, and the cone-shaped part grows from the flower, so it is a fruit. Judging by shape alone is the common mistake.
column29: Which trait is found only in one group?

column9: The Canada yew, a Wisconsin shrub, has no flowers. Each seed sits in a soft red cup that looks like a berry. Why do biologists still call the yew a gymnosperm?
column14: Because it has no flowers, so the red cup is not a true fruit and the seed is not enclosed
column15: Because any plant with red berries is a gymnosperm
column17: Because it has no vascular tissue
column28: True fruits come only from flowers. A yew has no flowers, and its red cup is open at the top, leaving the seed exposed. Calling any berry-looking part a fruit is the common mistake.
column29: Where do true fruits come from?

column9: Both ferns and mosses need water for their sperm to swim to the eggs, yet ferns can grow much taller than mosses. What explains the difference in height?
column14: Ferns make seeds and mosses do not
column15: Ferns have vascular tissue to move water up; mosses do not
column16: Ferns have flowers that hold water
column28: Height depends on vascular tissue, which ferns have and mosses lack. Saying ferns make seeds is the common mistake; ferns are seedless.
column29: Both are seedless. What do ferns have that mosses lack?

column9: Four plants are described. Plant A: no vascular tissue, spores. Plant B: vascular tissue, spores. Plant C: vascular tissue, seeds in cones. Plant D: vascular tissue, seeds in fruit. Which two plants make pollen?
column28: Pollen is made by seed plants, which are C (gymnosperm) and D (angiosperm). Picking B and C is the common mistake because both have vascular tissue, but B uses spores and makes no pollen.
column29: Pollen goes with seeds.

column9: A plant makes seeds inside fruit, and its leaves have parallel veins. Which other traits would you most likely find? Select all that apply.
column17: Vascular bundles in a ring in the stem
column28: Fruit plus parallel veins means a monocot, so expect flower parts in 3s, one cotyledon and fibrous roots. Bundles in a ring and two cotyledons are dicot traits, and cones belong to gymnosperms. Mixing monocot and dicot traits is the common mistake.
column29: First decide monocot or dicot from the veins.

column9: Which statements about xylem and phloem are correct? Select all that apply.
column14: Xylem carries water and minerals up from the roots
column15: Phloem carries sugar from the leaves to other parts of the plant
column16: Neither xylem nor phloem is found in mosses
column17: Phloem carries water up from the roots
column18: Xylem carries sugar down from the leaves
column28: Xylem moves water and minerals up, phloem moves sugar from the leaves, and mosses have neither. The last two choices swap the jobs of xylem and phloem, which is the most common mistake.
column29: One tissue moves water, the other moves food.

column9: A student coats every leaf of one bean plant, top and bottom, with petroleum jelly and leaves a second bean plant uncoated. After three days, the coated plant has lost much less water. What is the best explanation?
column14: The jelly added water to the leaves
column15: The jelly blocked the phloem in the stem
column16: The jelly blocked the stomata, so less water vapor could escape
column17: The jelly stopped the roots from absorbing water
column28: Water vapor leaves through the stomata, and the jelly sealed them. Blaming the roots is the common mistake; the jelly only touched the leaves.
column29: Where does water vapor leave a leaf?

column9: A student thinks that water evaporating from leaves helps pull water up a celery stalk. She puts a leafy celery stalk in blue dye for 3 hours. Which control would make this a fair test?
column14: A leafy celery stalk in plain water for 3 hours
column15: An identical celery stalk with its leaves removed, in the same dye for the same 3 hours
column16: A carrot with its leaves on, in the same dye for 3 hours
column17: A celery stalk with its leaves removed, in the dye overnight in a dark closet
column28: A fair test changes only one thing, the leaves, and keeps the dye, time and conditions the same. The last choice is the common trap because it also changes the time and the light.
column29: Change only the variable being tested.

column9: In spring, pine trees release huge yellow clouds of pollen, while apple trees make much less pollen but have bright, sweet-smelling flowers. What is the best explanation?
column14: Pine pollen is food for the pine seedlings
column15: Apple trees do not need pollen to make seeds
column16: Pine pollen is really spores, so more is needed
column17: Wind carries pine pollen and most of it is wasted, while insects carry apple pollen straight from flower to flower
column28: Wind pollination is hit-or-miss, so conifers make huge amounts of pollen. Bright, scented flowers attract insects that deliver pollen directly. Thinking pollen is food for the seed is a common mistake.
column29: Why would a flower need bright colors and a sweet smell?

column9: Robins eat the fruits of a wild black cherry tree and drop the seeds in their droppings far away. What does this show about why fruit is an advantage for angiosperms?
column14: Fruit attracts animals that carry the seeds away from the parent plant
column15: Fruit lets the seed carry out photosynthesis
column16: Fruit takes the place of vascular tissue
column17: Fruit lets the sperm swim to the egg
column28: Fruit attracts animals, which spread the seeds to new places where they do not compete with the parent. Thinking fruit feeds the parent plant is a common misunderstanding.
column29: Where do the seeds end up?

column9: Plants can be sorted with three yes-or-no questions: Vascular tissue? Seeds? Flowers? Plant 1 answers yes, yes, no. Plant 2 answers yes, no (and stops there). Which pair could these be?
column14: Plant 1 is a sugar maple and Plant 2 is a moss
column15: Plant 1 is a moss and Plant 2 is a fern
column16: Plant 1 is a white spruce and Plant 2 is an ostrich fern
column17: Plant 1 is a tulip and Plant 2 is a pine
column28: Yes, yes, no means a gymnosperm (spruce). Yes, no means vascular but seedless (fern). Choosing maple and moss is the common mistake; a maple has flowers, and a moss would answer no to the first question.
column29: Work through each answer one question at a time.

column9: Trillium has flower parts in 3s and one cotyledon, but its leaves have net-like veins. How should a biologist classify it?
column14: As a dicot, because leaf veins outrank every other trait
column15: As a gymnosperm, because it does not fit either group
column16: As a monocot, because most of its key traits are monocot traits
column17: As a fern, because it grows on the forest floor
column28: Biologists weigh several traits, and trillium's flower parts and single cotyledon mark it as a monocot. Letting one exception decide is the common mistake.
column29: Count how many traits point each way.

column9: A leaf has 300 stomata per mm² on its underside and 60 stomata per mm² on its top surface. What percent of the leaf's stomata are on the underside? Round to the nearest tenth.
column28: Total = 300 + 60 = 360. Underside share = 300 ÷ 360 × 100 = 83.3%. A common mistake is dividing 300 by 60 (which gives 5, a ratio, not a percent).
column29: Find the total first, then divide the underside count by the total.

column9: A green, many-celled organism is found in a pond. Which observation would show that it is a plant and not an alga?
column14: It has true roots, stems and leaves with xylem and phloem
column28: Algae also have chlorophyll, photosynthesize and have cell walls, so those traits cannot tell them apart. Vascular tissue and true organs are found only in plants. Picking photosynthesis is the common mistake.
column29: Which trait do plants have that algae never do?

column9: Which statements are true of BOTH gymnosperms and angiosperms? Select all that apply.
column18: Their new plants grow from spores released into the air
column28: Both groups are vascular seed plants that make pollen. Only angiosperms make fruit and flowers, and neither grows new plants from released spores. Choosing fruit is the common mistake.
column29: Find what all seed plants have in common.

column9: A student claims, "Plants get their food from the soil." A scientist grows a small willow tree in a pot for five years, adding only water. The tree gains more than 70 kg, but the soil loses only a few grams. Which conclusion is best supported?
column14: The tree got all of its food from the soil
column15: The tree's mass came from the pot
column16: The soil must have been replaced each year
column17: The tree's mass did not come from the soil, which fits the idea that plants make their own food
column28: The soil barely changed, so the tree's growth came from elsewhere: plants build sugar from carbon dioxide and water using light. Thinking roots take in food from the soil is the common misconception.
column29: Compare how much the tree gained with how much the soil lost.

column9: Maple, ash and dogwood are the common Wisconsin trees with opposite leaves. A student finds a tree with two leaves across from each other at every node, and each leaf is made of 7 leaflets on a central stalk. Which tree is it most likely to be?
column28: Opposite leaves narrow it to maple, ash or dogwood, and a compound leaf with leaflets points to ash. Sugar maple is the common wrong answer; its leaves are opposite but simple, one piece.
column29: Which opposite-leaved tree has compound leaves?

column9: Pine needles are narrow and covered in a thick waxy cuticle. Why does this help a pine stay green through a Wisconsin winter?
column14: It cuts water loss when the ground is frozen and the roots cannot take in water
column15: It lets snow melt into the needles
column16: It lets more water evaporate to cool the tree
column17: It lets the needles make seeds in winter
column28: In winter the frozen soil makes water hard to get, so needles that lose very little water can stay alive. Thinking the wax helps the needles absorb water is the common mistake; wax keeps water in.
column29: Can roots take in water from frozen ground?

column9: Which is the best evidence that a sugar maple and a white pine are more closely related to each other than either is to a moss?
column15: Both have vascular tissue and make seeds
column28: Vascular tissue and seeds are shared traits that mosses lack. Green color and oxygen release are true of mosses too, and where a plant grows says nothing about how related it is.
column29: Find traits that the moss does NOT have.

column9: Match each type of conifer leaf to its description and example.
column14: Scale-like :: Tiny leaves that overlap like shingles, as on northern white cedar
column15: Linear :: Single flat needles growing one at a time, as on balsam fir
column16: Fascicled :: Bundles of 2 to 5 needles wrapped at the base by a sheath, as on pines
column17: Clustered :: Tufts of many needles on short spurs with no sheath, as on tamarack
column28: Cedar has scale-like leaves, fir has single linear needles, pine needles come in sheathed bundles (fascicles) and tamarack needles grow in clusters on spurs. Mixing up fascicled and clustered is the common mistake; only fascicles have a sheath.
column29: Fascicle means bundle. Which tree's needles come in wrapped bundles?

column9: Match each leaf type to its description.
column14: Simple :: One continuous piece of leaf tissue
column15: Pinnately compound :: Leaflets arranged along both sides of a central stalk
column16: Bipinnately compound :: Leaflets on side stalks that branch off a central stalk
column17: Palmately compound :: Leaflets that all attach at one point, like fingers on a hand
column28: Simple is one piece, pinnate leaflets line a stalk, bipinnate has leaflets on side stalks and palmate leaflets spread from one point. Mixing up pinnate and palmate is the common mistake.
column29: Palm means the palm of your hand.

column9: A student classifies a sugar maple with a key that asks about the broadest trait (shared by the most plant groups) first and the narrowest trait last. Put the steps in order, ending with the answer.
column14: Ask: Does it have flowers and fruit? (Yes, its seeds are inside winged fruits.)
column15: Conclude: The sugar maple is an angiosperm.
column16: Ask: Does it make seeds? (Yes, its winged seeds.)
column17: Ask: Does it have vascular tissue? (Yes, it grows tall.)
column28: The questions go from the oldest trait to the newest: vascular tissue, then seeds, then flowers and fruit. Only after all three can you conclude angiosperm. Asking about flowers first skips the traits that rule out mosses and ferns.
column29: Start with the trait that separates mosses from all other plants.
